title: Python venv / pipx — Installing Tools on Modern Kali
body:
Modern Kali (and Debian 12+) ships PEP 668, which BLOCKS system-wide pip with an 'externally-managed-environment' error. This trips people up constantly when a cloned tool says 'pip install -r requirements.txt' and it refuses. There are three correct ways to install Python tooling, and picking the right one saves a lot of frustration.

1. pipx — the right choice for standalone CLI tools (certipy, impacket, mitm6, bloodhound-python). It auto-creates an isolated venv per tool and puts the command on your PATH, so there's no activate/deactivate dance. Install once, use anywhere.

2. venv — the right choice when you git clone a repo that has its own requirements.txt. You create an isolated environment, activate it, install the repo's deps into it, run the tool, then deactivate. Keeps a tool's dependencies from colliding with your system or other tools.

3. --break-system-packages — the quick-and-dirty escape hatch. It forces pip to install system-wide anyway. Fine on a throwaway lab VM when you just need it now; avoid it on a system you care about because it can break apt-managed Python packages.

Rule of thumb: a CLI tool you'll reuse → pipx. A cloned repo with requirements.txt → venv. A one-off you don't care about → --break-system-packages.
cmd:
# ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# pipx — standalone CLI tools (best default for offensive tooling)
# ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
sudo apt install -y pipx
pipx ensurepath          # adds ~/.local/bin to PATH (restart shell after)
pipx install certipy-ad
pipx install impacket
pipx install mitm6
pipx list                # see what's installed
pipx upgrade-all

# ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# venv — for a cloned repo with its own requirements.txt
# ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
git clone https://github.com/SomeRepo/tool && cd tool
python3 -m venv .venv            # create the env (named .venv here)
source .venv/bin/activate        # activate — prompt shows (.venv)
pip install -r requirements.txt  # installs INTO the venv (no PEP668 error)
python3 tool.py                  # run it while activated
deactivate                       # leave the env when done

# next time you use the tool, just re-activate:
source .venv/bin/activate

# ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# --break-system-packages — quick + dirty (throwaway VMs only)
# ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
pip install <package> --break-system-packages
pip3 install impacket --break-system-packages

# ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# apt is still cleanest when the tool is packaged
# ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y seclists impacket-scripts netexec chisel
warn: If 'pipx: command not found' after install, restart your shell (pipx ensurepath edited your rc file). If an activated venv 'can't find' a system tool, that's expected — venvs isolate Python packages, not system binaries. And don't reach for --break-system-packages as a default: it can clobber apt-managed packages and leave your Kali Python in a bad state. pipx or venv first.
